title: A Forbidden Classroom Management Strategy You Should Be Using https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/08/21/a-forbidden-classroom-management-strategy/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin reclaims repetition, the much-maligned 'drill and kill' technique, as an essential classroom management tool for teaching routines and procedures. He distinguishes drilling academic content, which can dampen enthusiasm, from practicing physical-and-mental routines like lining up or entering the classroom, which he argues can only be mastered through repeated practice. He warns that repetition becomes counterproductive in the hands of an impatient teacher who makes students feel punished, and instead offers guidelines for doing it well: frame it as 'practice' like a sports team, teach and model first, space repetitions across the day rather than drilling endlessly, praise during practice and save critique for afterward, and stop repeating once students get it right. Linsin frames mastering routines as ultimately a matter of pride—both in doing something well and in belonging to a well-functioning class—rather than mere compliance.
points: Distinguish 'drill and kill' academic repetition, which can dampen learning, from practicing physical classroom routines, which requires repetition to master.
Frame repeated practice as sports-style 'practice' rather than punishment, and always teach and model a routine before asking students to repeat it.
Practice each routine only twice in a row, then return to it later in the day or the next day rather than drilling it to exhaustion.
Offer immediate praise during practice, save detailed critique for after the routine is finished, and stop repeating once students get it right.
Treat well-executed routines as a source of student pride and identity, not just an efficiency measure.
quotes: The forbidden strategy I’m referring to has gotten a bad rap, but is so effective it’s used to train nurses, police officers, professional athletes, and opera singers.
In the hands of an unskilled or impatient teacher, students can become bored, resentful, and likely to cause trouble.
Repetition should come only after baseline learning takes place. Teach and model routines thoroughly before asking students to practice them.
Practice each routine only twice in a row. Then take a break from that particular routine. Your students will learn faster if you come back and practice later in the day—or the next one.
Only repeat a routine done incorrectly. If your students get it right, tell them they were perfect and move on to something else.
Routines are about pride—pride in doing something well, pride in being part of a special group, and pride in standing apart from the crowd.
